volumes.title: The Brass Plate
volumes.text:
I came to Hollowmere on the first of October, with two crates of books, a new brass plate and old Dr. Pell's bag, which he pressed on me when he retired to the Grey Coast. The village lies where the marsh road meets the Emberwick road: forty houses and a duck pond. Mrs. Ardle keeps the doctor's house and regards me as a temporary arrangement.

For three days nobody called. The village had had Dr. Pell for forty-one years and saw no reason to be ill for a stranger. I polished the plate. I learned the pony's name, which is Bramble, and her opinion of me, which is low.

On the fourth day a boy named Davy Fenn knocked, holding out a thumb with a splinter in it. I drew it with a needle and he did not cry. He inspected the splinter, then me, and said he would tell the others I was all right.

volumes.title: The Blacksmith's Cough
volumes.text:
Casebook of Tobias Quince, physician at Hollowmere, late October. Amos Garth the blacksmith came to my door today, sent by his wife and walking like a man to the dentist. He has had a cough for three weeks. It sounds like a dog fox barking in a barrel.

I listened to his chest and found it sound. Then I walked down to see his forge, which told me more than his chest had. He had closed every shutter against the cold, and the smoke hung under the rafters like a second ceiling.

My advice was open shutters, a walk along the marsh road at noon, and honey in something hot at bedtime. He paid me by mending my gate latch. Three weeks on, the cough is gone. Amos tells everyone it went away by itself. Mrs. Ardle, my housekeeper, says that in this village there is no higher praise.

volumes.title: Mrs. Tansy's Thursdays
volumes.text:
I am Tobias Quince, six weeks the doctor at Hollowmere, and Mrs. Tansy has sent for me five times. First it was her knee, then an ear, then a fluttering, then the knee again. Each time I found nothing wrong and the tea already laid for two.

It took me until November to make the diagnosis. Her sister moved to the Lowlands in the spring, and the cottage is very quiet. That is not a thing one can write on a slip of paper and hand across a table.

So I told her that her neighbour Miss Pilbeam, who is growing deaf, needed someone to read aloud to her each Thursday, as exercise for the ears. I told Miss Pilbeam that Mrs. Tansy needed company and must not know it. Both have improved wonderfully. I still call there, but as a guest, and the cake has improved too.

volumes.title: The Night Ride
volumes.text:
Hollowmere, midwinter. At two this morning Jem Fenny hammered on my door: the baby was coming, out at Fenny Farm, three miles along the marsh causeway. I saddled Bramble by lantern light. The pony made her feelings plain, but she went, and the frost rang under her like iron.

I arrived to find Nan Sorrel already there. She has been the village midwife since before I was born, and she had everything in hand. She looked me over, the new young doctor with ice on his eyebrows, and gave me two tasks: keep the kettle full and keep the father out of the way.

I walked Jem round the yard eleven times. At first light his daughter arrived, loud and pink and perfectly well, and her mother with her. They have named her Hester. I did nothing but hold a lantern, and I have seldom been so glad to be anywhere.

volumes.title: The Schoolmaster Cannot Sleep
volumes.text:
Casebook of Dr. Tobias Quince, Hollowmere, January. Mr. Lorimer the schoolmaster came to me grey under the eyes. He cannot sleep. He lies awake counting what might go wrong: the inspector's visit, the schoolroom roof, the Fenn boys and the inkwells. He asked for a sleeping draught.

I gave him three instructions instead. No ledgers after supper. A walk to the duck pond and back before bed, whatever the weather. And his worries were to be written each night on a slate and left downstairs, where they would keep perfectly well until morning.

He plainly thought it poor value. But a fortnight later he stopped me by the pump to report that he now sleeps until the cock crows. The slate, he says, carries the same three worries most nights, and they look a good deal smaller in chalk. The Fenn boys remain beyond the reach of medicine.

volumes.title: The Postman's Ankle
volumes.text:
February, Hollowmere. Ned Harrow the postman went down on the ice beside the pump and could not get up. A sprain, I found, not a break, but the ankle swelled like a turnip. I bound it and ordered him to keep it up on a stool for a week. He took the sprain bravely. The thought of the letters nearly finished him.

So for seven days the post went round with the doctor. Bramble the pony and I carried the bag on my rounds, and I learned the parish as no casebook could teach it: which gates stick, which dogs mean it, who hears from the Lowlands every week and who never hears from anyone.

People who would not have called me to a sickbed talked for ten minutes over a letter. By the time Ned was walking, I had stood at every door in the village. He says I delivered two letters wrongly. He is right.

volumes.title: The Speckles
volumes.text:
Casebook of Tobias Quince, village doctor at Hollowmere. April brought what the village calls the speckles: pink spots, a mild fever and a mighty itch. It began with the Fenn children and went through the school like a rumour. Nineteen cases in ten days.

There is little a doctor can do for the speckles except visit. I went from cottage to cottage and said the same things: keep them home, keep them cool and quiet, give them broth, and stop them scratching. The mothers knew all this already. I think my use was to say it would pass, in the voice of someone holding a bag.

It passed. All nineteen were out of bed within the fortnight. Davy Fenn tried to count his spots and reached sixty-four before he lost his place. The school was shut for ten days, and Mr. Lorimer the schoolmaster told me, in confidence, that he had never felt better.

volumes.title: Hay for Silas Croft
volumes.text:
Hollowmere, June. Silas Croft has put his back out, and he chose the first day of haymaking to do it. I found him bent like a hairpin beside his own gate. A week of rest would mend him, I said. He said the hay would not wait a week, and that I knew less about farming than his dog.

He was right about the hay. So that evening I went round the village, not as a doctor exactly, and mentioned the matter at seven or eight doors.

Next morning there were eleven people in Croft's meadow with scythes and rakes, the blacksmith among them. The field was cut, turned and carted in three days. Silas watched from a mattress by the gate, shouting directions nobody followed. His back is mended now. Rest is the hardest thing to prescribe to a farmer, and the patient cannot always fill the prescription alone.

volumes.title: Bramble Goes Lame
volumes.text:
July. I am Tobias Quince, doctor at Hollowmere, and my pony Bramble is the patient this month. She picked up a stone on the marsh road and bruised her foot. Amos Garth the blacksmith looked at it, ordered a fortnight's rest in the paddock, and told me not to argue, in very much my own voice.

So I walked my rounds, six miles on a short day. I expected to fall behind. Instead the village rearranged itself around me. Those who could walk came to the surgery to spare my legs. Children carried my bag in relays from one cottage to the next. The Crofts offered me their donkey, which I declined with thanks, having met it.

Mrs. Tansy sent a pie to keep my strength up. Bramble is sound again, and no better tempered. But for a fortnight I was looked after by my own patients, and I have not forgotten it.

volumes.title: Dr. Pell Comes to Tea
volumes.text:
Hollowmere, August. Old Dr. Pell came over from the Grey Coast today, to see what I have done with his village. He was doctor here for forty-one years before me. He studied my brass plate, then his old bag, which I still carry, and then me.

We walked down the street together and it took an hour, because every door opened. Over tea he asked what I, Tobias Quince, had learned in ten months, and I began to list remedies. He let me finish.

"What I learned," he said, "is that most people will tell you what is wrong in the first minute, if you let them reach the end of the sentence. Listen first. The bag is mainly for carrying sandwiches." Then he told me he had it on good authority that I was all right. The authority was Davy Fenn. He went home on the carrier's cart, looking content.

volumes.title: Plums at the Harvest Supper
volumes.text:
Casebook of Tobias Quince, Hollowmere, September. The harvest supper was held in Croft's barn, and I was put at the top table, between Nan Sorrel the midwife and Mr. Lorimer the schoolmaster. A year ago I would have been lucky to get a stool by the door.

Halfway through the goose, a small hand tugged my sleeve. Davy Fenn was underneath the table, and green. He had a pain in his middle. Under questioning he admitted to plums, and under further questioning to seventeen of them.

I prescribed lying down in the hay, nothing more to eat, and time. By the first dance he was upright again and watching the pudding with interest. Later Amos Garth the blacksmith stood up and proposed the health of the doctor. I looked round for Dr. Pell. It was a moment before I understood that he meant me.

volumes.title: The Doctor Takes to Bed
volumes.text:
October again, and a year since I, Tobias Quince, came to Hollowmere. I marked the occasion by catching a heavy cold on the marsh road. Mrs. Ardle, my housekeeper, ordered me to bed in words I recognised as my own.

Then the village arrived. Mrs. Tansy sent broth. Honey came from Fenny Farm. Amos Garth eased my bedroom shutter so that it would open, for the air, on doctor's orders. Ned Harrow brought the post upstairs. Nan Sorrel inspected me and said I would live, and Davy Fenn stood in the doorway to confirm that I was all right.

I was up in four days. That afternoon I opened the last crate of books, which had stood nailed shut in the hall for a year, in case I should not stay. Mrs. Ardle watched me shelve them. Then she said she supposed she had better order coal for the winter, and for the one after.

volumes.title: January: Honey
volumes.text:
I am Philippa Yarrow, and I keep the remedy shop at the sign of the Green Jar in Emberwick. This January I took an apprentice, Colm Reddy, aged thirteen. He arrived hoping for powdered pearls and dragon's teeth. I showed him the shelves: forty jars of honey, dried mint, and a great deal of barley.

His first customer was the carter, with a throat like a rusty hinge. Colm looked to me for something rare. I had him stir a spoonful of honey into a cup of warm water with a slice of lemon, and send the man home to sip it and keep quiet for a day.

Honey cures nothing, I told Colm afterwards. It soothes, which is a different trade and an honest one. A sore throat mends in its own time, and our business is to make the waiting kinder. He wrote that down, looking cheated. He will come round.

volumes.title: February: Broth
volumes.text:
February at the Green Jar, my remedy shop in Emberwick. The cold weather has half of Tallow Lane in bed, and my apprentice Colm asked which jar on our shelves was best for people too weak to get up. I told him the best remedy for that was not in a jar. It was in the big black pot.

Broth is a chicken, an onion, a carrot and a handful of barley, left to simmer until the kitchen window runs with steam. It asks nothing of a tired body and gives back warmth, salt and the sense of being looked after. I think the last of these does most of the work.

Our pot goes up the lane each winter from house to house, and comes back washed, with a different thank-you in it every time. This week it returned holding six eggs. Colm carried it out twice in the sleet and did not complain, which I have noted in his favour.

volumes.title: March: Fresh Air
volumes.text:
I am Philippa Yarrow of the Green Jar in Emberwick, and in March I prescribe what costs nothing. A young clerk came in this week, pale as a candle, complaining of a heavy head and no appetite. My apprentice Colm reached hopefully for the tonic shelf.

I asked the clerk where he worked. In a back office, it turned out, with the window painted shut and a stove going from eight until six. I sold him nothing. I told him to walk the river path to the ferry and back every noon, and to have that window unstuck by a carpenter.

Colm thought we had lost a sale. But sickrooms, offices and bedrooms all go stale, and a stale room makes a dull head. A window open a hand's breadth is a remedy as old as windows. The clerk came back in a fortnight with colour in his face, and bought honey he did not need, out of gratitude.

volumes.title: April: The Elixir Man
volumes.text:
April brought a painted wagon to Emberwick market, and with it Professor Lucian Vesper and his Universal Elixir, in purple bottles. It cured, he announced, coughs, corns, melancholy, baldness and the bad temper of horses. My apprentice Colm stood in the front row with his mouth open. Our own shop, the Green Jar, has never claimed to cure even one of those.

I bought a bottle, for science. Back at my counter I tasted it: sugar water, coloured with something and flavoured with liquorice. Quite harmless. Rather pleasant, in fact.

Colm asked why I did not denounce the man in the square. I said the elixir would hurt nothing but purses, and that people forgive a fraud sooner than a scold. But I told him to watch what a remedy promises. The honest ones promise very little. The professor drove on toward the Lowlands, a little ahead of his customers.

volumes.title: May: Sleep
volumes.text:
May, at the Green Jar in Emberwick. The miller's wife came in grey with tiredness. She has not slept properly in a month, since the new mill clock arrived, and she wanted the strongest thing I had. I am Philippa Yarrow, and the strongest thing I have for sleeplessness is a list.

A warm cup of milk at bedtime. A small bag of dried lavender under the pillow, which smells of summer and does no more than that. No accounts after supper. And the clock was to be carried down to the kitchen, where it could tick at the cat.

My apprentice Colm sewed the lavender bag himself, with stitches like a row of fence posts. Sleep cannot be forced, I told him. It can only be invited, and it comes soonest to a quiet room. The miller's wife called in a week later to say she had slept nine hours. The cat, she says, is looking tired.

volumes.title: June: Barley Water
volumes.text:
Haymaking began this week around Emberwick, and with it my busiest trade of the summer, which is in barley water. I am Philippa Yarrow of the Green Jar, and every June I send my apprentice out to the meadows with two stone jars slung on a yoke.

Barley water is only barley simmered, strained and cooled, with a little lemon and honey to make it welcome. There is no magic in it. But men will mow all day under a hot sun and forget to drink, and by afternoon their heads ache and their tempers go.

Colm came back sunburnt and thoughtful. He had found old Hobson dizzy by the hedge and had sat him in the shade with a wet cloth on his neck and a cup in his hand, without being told. In half an hour the old man was himself again. Shade, water and sitting down: Colm is beginning to see how plain most remedies are.

volumes.title: July: Mint
volumes.text:
The day after the Emberwick summer fair is always the same at the Green Jar. By nine o'clock there is a row of sorry faces at my counter, each of whom ate a pie too many, or the toffee apples on top of the pickled eggs. I am Philippa Yarrow, and I keep a large jar of dried mint for exactly this morning.

A pinch of mint in a cup, hot water over it, and five minutes' patience. It smells clean and it settles a stomach that has merely been overworked. I had my apprentice Colm make eleven cups before noon.

He asked what else we might give them. Nothing, I said. A stomach that has been insulted wants a quiet day and plain food, and it will forgive by evening. The mint is mostly a kindness to sip while it does. Colm drank the twelfth cup himself. He had been at the fair too, and the toffee apples.

volumes.title: August: Colm's Great Tonic
volumes.text:
August is slow at the Green Jar, my remedy shop in Emberwick, and I left my apprentice Colm in charge for an afternoon. He has never forgotten the travelling professor and his Universal Elixir. I came home to a smell like a pond in a heatwave.

Colm had made a tonic. His reasoning was that if mint is good, and honey, and barley, and lavender, and ginger, and stewed apple, then all of them boiled together in one pot must be six times as good. The result was grey. It had a skin on it. The shop cat had left by the window.

Nobody was harmed, because nobody could be persuaded to taste it, Colm included. I asked what it was meant to cure. "Everything," he said. That, I told him, is the fault in it. A remedy for everything is a remedy for nothing in particular. We poured it on the rhubarb, which has not complained.

volumes.title: September: Plain Food
volumes.text:
September, and the Green Jar smells of apples. I am Philippa Yarrow, remedy-keeper of Emberwick, and this month my apprentice Colm learned what to give people who are nearly well.

Old Mrs. Finch has been three weeks in bed with a chest cold. The cold has gone, but she is weak as a kitten and cannot face her dinner. Her daughter wanted a strengthening tonic. I sent Colm round instead with a bowl of apples stewed soft, and the next day with oat porridge and a spoon of honey in the middle.

Getting better is its own piece of work, I explained, and the body wants plain fuel for it: soft, warm, and little at a time. Appetite comes back like a shy cat, and must not be rushed at with roast beef. On the fifth day Mrs. Finch asked for a boiled egg and complained that the toast was cold. Complaining is an excellent sign.

volumes.title: October: Warmth
volumes.text:
The first frost came to Emberwick this week and brought the usual visitors to the Green Jar: people with chills, stiff knees and cold feet that will not warm. I am Philippa Yarrow, and October is when I fetch the river stones down from the attic.

A smooth stone, warmed by the hearth and wrapped in two thicknesses of flannel, will keep a bed warm for half the night. I lend them out by the dozen. For the rest, a wool shawl, thick stockings, and a cup of hot water with a slice of ginger, which warms from the inside.

My apprentice Colm wrapped stones all Tuesday. He remarked that we had sold nothing all day and had lent nearly everything. I said that was a fair description of the trade. Then he took a stone round to the old ferryman without being asked, and I began to think the shop would be safe with him.

volumes.title: November: Company
volumes.text:
In November a painted wagon limped into Emberwick with one lamp out. It was Professor Vesper, seller of the Universal Elixir, and he had a streaming cold, a cough and nowhere to stay. His own purple bottles had done nothing for him. I am Philippa Yarrow of the Green Jar, and I put him in my back room.

My apprentice Colm nursed him with everything this year has taught us: honey for the throat, broth from the black pot, a warm stone at his feet and the window open a hand's breadth. Mostly, though, Colm sat and listened to his stories. The professor has been alone on the road for eleven years.

On the fourth day he confessed, unasked, that his elixir was sugar water. We said we knew. He was better by the week's end, and I believe the listening did as much as the broth. He now sells honey drops in the market, and calls them only honey drops.

volumes.title: December: The Universal Tonic
volumes.text:
December, the last page of my year at the Green Jar in Emberwick. On Midwinter Eve my apprentice Colm Reddy handed me a sheet of our best paper. He had finally written out his Universal Tonic, and he asked me, Philippa Yarrow, to judge it.

It read: Honey for the throat. Broth for the weak. Fresh air for the dull head. Sleep, invited and not forced. Water in the heat and warmth in the cold. Plain food, a little at a time. Someone to sit by the bed. And time, which does most of the mending and takes none of the credit.

Not one item needs a purple bottle. I could find nothing to add, so I framed it and hung it over the counter. Then I gave Colm the key to the still-room. He came in January looking for dragon's teeth. He has found something better, and he knows it.

volumes.title: Introducing Mr. Pym
volumes.text:
This manual is written for my apprentice, Nell Wicker, who came to my surgery in Tanner's Row, Emberwick, at the age of fifteen, wishing to learn bones. I am Dr. Augustin Farrow. I have set them for thirty years.

Our teacher in these pages is Mr. Pym. He hangs from a hook beside my desk: a full skeleton carved in pearwood by a cabinetmaker who owed me for a mended wrist. Every bone is there to the proper size, two hundred and six in all, counting the six tiny ear bones we keep in a pillbox. Or rather two hundred and five. His left kneecap went missing years ago, and I suspect a dog.

A grown person has two hundred and six bones. A newborn baby has nearer three hundred pieces, many still soft, which knit together as the child grows. We shall take Mr. Pym from the top down. Nell has already shaken his hand.

volumes.title: The Skull's Seams
volumes.text:
Nell Wicker, my apprentice, supposed the skull to be one bone, like a pot. I, Dr. Farrow of Emberwick, lifted down the head of Mr. Pym, our pearwood skeleton, and showed her the seams. A skull is twenty-two bones. Eight make the rounded case that keeps the brain, and fourteen make the face. They lock along wavy joins, like well-cut pieces of a puzzle. Only the lower jaw is free to move.

In a baby those seams are not yet closed, and there is a soft place on the crown that fills in during the second year. A head must have room to grow.

This week the cooper's boy stood up under a beam and raised a lump like a hen's egg. His mother feared the worst. I found a sound skull, a clear eye and a boy keen to describe the beam. He was kept quiet for a day and watched, and that was all.

volumes.title: Hammer, Anvil, Stirrup
volumes.text:
The smallest bones of the body live in a pillbox in my desk drawer, and I let my apprentice Nell Wicker tip them into her palm. They belong to Mr. Pym, the pearwood skeleton of my surgery in Emberwick. There are three for each ear, named for their shapes: the hammer, the anvil and the stirrup.

They sit in a chain behind the eardrum. When a sound sets the drum trembling, the hammer passes the tremble to the anvil, and the anvil to the stirrup, which hands it inward to be heard. The stirrup is the smallest bone we own, no bigger than a grain of rice. The cabinetmaker who carved Mr. Pym said those six cost him more trouble than both legs.

Old Mr. Dabney came in today, quite sure his family had taken to mumbling. Age, not illness; hearing wears as knees do. I, Dr. Farrow, could offer him only an ear trumpet and my sympathy, loudly.

volumes.title: Seven in the Neck
volumes.text:
To teach the spine I, Dr. Farrow, had my apprentice Nell run a finger down the back of Mr. Pym, the pearwood skeleton who hangs in our Emberwick surgery, counting as she went. Seven bones in the neck. Twelve in the back, each carrying a pair of ribs. Five large ones in the loins. That makes twenty-four that move. Below them sits the sacrum, five bones grown into one, and last the little tailbone.

Between each moving pair lies a cushion of gristle, so the column can bend and take a jolt. The cushions settle through the day; we are all a shade taller at breakfast than at supper. A giraffe, I am told, has seven neck bones too, only longer.

The weaver came in this week, stiff as his own loom from sitting. His spine was sound. I advised him to stand and stretch whenever he finished a hand's breadth of cloth. Backs are made to move.

volumes.title: Twelve Pairs of Ribs
volumes.text:
My apprentice Nell Wicker asked whether men have one rib fewer than women, as her grandmother holds. I am Dr. Farrow of Emberwick, and I let our pearwood skeleton, Mr. Pym, answer. She counted him: twelve ribs on each side, twenty-four in all. It is the same for everyone.

The ribs make a cage for the heart and lungs. The upper seven pairs join the breastbone in front. The next three pairs each hang from the rib above. The last two pairs are short and join nothing in front; we call them floating ribs. The whole cage lifts and widens with each breath, which Nell proved with her hands on her own sides.

The thatcher slid off a roof into a hay cart and bruised three ribs. Nothing was broken. Bruised ribs want only rest and time, and the difficulty is laughing. He begged his friends to stop visiting, since every one arrived with a joke.

volumes.title: The Collarbone
volumes.text:
Run a finger from your throat out to your shoulder and you are tracing the collarbone. I, Dr. Farrow, showed it to my apprentice Nell on Mr. Pym, the pearwood skeleton of our surgery in Emberwick. It is slender and gently curved, like a long letter S, and it works as a strut, holding the shoulder out from the chest so the arm can swing free. Behind it lies the shoulder blade, a flat triangle that glides over the back of the ribs.

Being a strut, the collarbone takes the shock when anyone lands on an outstretched hand. It is the bone I see broken most often, and children mend it fastest.

The carrier's daughter came off her pony on Saturday and broke hers cleanly. I put the arm in a sling, and Nell tied the knot. In a few weeks there will be a small firm lump where the bone has knitted, and the girl intends to show it to everyone.

volumes.title: The Arm and Its Hinge
volumes.text:
This page of the manual concerns the arm. I am Dr. Farrow of Tanner's Row, Emberwick, and I taught it to my apprentice Nell by unhooking the arm of Mr. Pym, our pearwood skeleton, and laying it across her knees.

From shoulder to elbow there is one stout bone. From elbow to wrist there are two, lying side by side: one on the thumb side and one on the side of the little finger. The second makes the hard point of the elbow. When you turn your palm downward, the thumb-side bone rolls across the other, and Nell turned Mr. Pym's hand over and back until she had seen it.

She asked for the funny bone. There is none. That tingle comes from a nerve crossing the back of the elbow, close under the skin. The baker's boy came in holding his elbow, certain it was broken. He had struck that nerve on a doorpost. He recovered while describing it.

volumes.title: Twenty-Seven in a Hand
volumes.text:
I asked my apprentice Nell Wicker to guess how many bones are in one hand. She said ten. So I, Dr. Farrow, unhooked the hand of Mr. Pym, the pearwood skeleton of our Emberwick surgery, and we counted. Eight small bones in the wrist, packed in two rows of four like cobbles. Five in the palm. Fourteen in the fingers: three to each finger and two to the thumb. Twenty-seven.

So many small pieces let the hand cup, grip, pinch and spread. A paw of ten bones could hold a spade, but it could not thread a needle.

Jory the fiddler came in with a sprained wrist, four days before the harvest dance, and in despair. Nothing was broken. I bound the wrist and forbade the fiddle for a fortnight. He stood on a barrel at the dance and whistled every tune instead, and Nell says no one stopped dancing.

volumes.title: The Longest Bone
volumes.text:
The thighbone is the longest and strongest bone we have. I, Dr. Farrow, measured Mr. Pym's against my apprentice Nell: in most people it is about a quarter of their whole height. Mr. Pym is the pearwood skeleton who hangs in our surgery in Emberwick, and his thighbones are the only parts of him that needed a second plank.

At its top the thighbone ends in a ball, set off on a short neck. The ball sits in a deep cup in the hip bone. The two hip bones meet the base of the spine to form a sturdy basin, which carries the weight of everything above.

Old Grandfather Oake's hips have grown stiff with age, and no doctor can make them young. But Nell cut him a blackthorn stick of the proper height, and he now walks to the bridge and back daily to show it off.

volumes.title: The Missing Kneecap
volumes.text:
Mr. Pym, the pearwood skeleton of my surgery in Emberwick, has no left kneecap. My apprentice Nell Wicker noticed it on her first day and has not let the matter rest. I am Dr. Farrow, and I admit it went missing in my time.

The kneecap is a small rounded shield of bone. It does not join the other bones directly. It rides inside the strong cord that runs from the thigh muscle to the shin, guarding the front of the knee and giving the muscle a better pull. A baby's kneecaps are soft gristle and harden into bone during childhood.

Mrs. Lunn the baker has a sore knee from kneeling to her low oven. I advised a cushion and a taller stool. Meanwhile Nell has searched the cupboards, the coal scuttle and the garden bed. No kneecap. She has asked the cabinetmaker for an offcut of pearwood, and will not say why.

volumes.title: Shin, Ankle and Arch
volumes.text:
Below the knee there are two bones again, I told my apprentice Nell Wicker, pointing them out on Mr. Pym, the pearwood skeleton of our Emberwick surgery. The shinbone is the stout one in front and bears the weight. Beside it runs a slender partner, thin as a flute. The knob on the inside of your ankle is the end of the first; the knob on the outside is the end of the second.

Then the foot: twenty-six bones. Seven make the ankle and heel, five the long middle, fourteen the toes. They are built into springy arches. Nell did a sum on the slate. Two hands and two feet hold one hundred and six bones, more than half the body's count.

Ned the postman came in with aching feet. I, Dr. Farrow, examined them and then his boots, which were worn flat as planks. I prescribed a cobbler.

volumes.title: How Bones Mend
volumes.text:
This is the last page of the manual I, Dr. Augustin Farrow, have written for my apprentice Nell Wicker, and it holds the best thing I know about bones. They are alive. A broken bone, set straight and kept still, builds a soft bridge across the break, and over some weeks the bridge hardens into new bone. The doctor only holds the ends in place. The bone does the mending.

Yesterday Nell stood before Mr. Pym, the pearwood skeleton of our surgery in Emberwick, and named all his bones from the crown to the smallest toe without one mistake. Then she took something from her apron pocket. She had carved a left kneecap from an offcut of pearwood, and it fits him exactly.

So Mr. Pym has two hundred and six bones at last, and I have a colleague instead of an apprentice. The old kneecap turned up this morning, behind the dresser. We have kept hers.

volumes.title: The First Lantern
volumes.text:
I am Clementine Rook, physician of Emberwick, and I begin this book on the eighth of November because of a boy's face. Tam Weller, the ferryman's son, was put to bed this afternoon with cheeks as red as a lamp behind a shade. His grandmother calls it the lantern fever, and says it comes through the town every dozen years or so.

A fever is not the illness itself. It is the body's own fire, lit on purpose against an unwelcome guest, and a sign that the household is defending itself. The doctor's work is mostly to keep the patient comfortable while the fire does its job.

Tam was hot, cross and thirsty, and otherwise sound. I ordered bed, water and a quiet room. Then I came home and ruled this book into columns, for I do not think he will be the only one. I mean to set down everything this fever does, from first case to last.

volumes.title: The Shiver
volumes.text:
Casebook of Dr. Clementine Rook, Emberwick, the tenth of November. A second case of the lantern fever today: Mrs. Dunnock, the baker's wife. I record how it begins, for it begins oddly. A fever starts with cold.

She had been kneading at the warm end of the bakery when she began to shiver. By the time I came she lay under three quilts with her teeth knocking together, declaring the house was freezing. Her forehead was hot as a new loaf. The body is stoking its fire, and while it stokes, the patient feels only the draught.

The shiver lasts an hour or two and is frightening to watch, though it does no harm. I sat with her until the chattering eased. Her husband hovered with a fourth quilt. Then, just as with young Tam Weller two days ago, the cold fit passed and the red cheeks came up like lamps being lit.

volumes.title: The Heat
volumes.text:
The second day of the lantern fever is the hot one. I am Dr. Clementine Rook of Emberwick, and I set down here what I saw in Tam Weller, the ferryman's boy, who was the first to take it.

His skin was dry and burning, his eyes very bright, his cheeks two red lamps. He was restless and wanted nothing, then wanted everything. His pulse ran quick as a pony trotting. This is the fire at full blaze, and though it alarms a household, it is the fever doing its work.

I have no wish to put the fire out, only to keep the patient easy beside it. A light sheet in place of blankets. A cool damp cloth on the forehead, changed when it warms. The window open a hand's breadth. Sips of water, often. His grandmother did all of it before I could say it. I sat and counted his breathing, which was steady.

volumes.title: The Thirst
volumes.text:
Emberwick, the fifteenth of November. The lantern fever has reached old Mr. Hobb, caretaker at the school in Lamp Lane, and from him I, Dr. Clementine Rook, have learned about the thirst.

A fevered body dries like washing in a wind. The lips crack, the tongue furs, and the patient thinks of nothing but drink. Water, then, in small sips and often; barley water; weak tea gone cool. I ask each household to keep a covered jug by the bed, and to offer the cup rather than wait to be asked.

Fever makes the thirsty particular. Mrs. Dunnock would take water only from her blue cup. Tam Weller asked for water from the middle of the river. Mr. Hobb demanded snow, in a week with none. His wife brought well water in a bowl and told him it was melted. He drank it and pronounced it excellent.

volumes.title: Fever Dreams
volumes.text:
On the third night of the lantern fever the mind wanders a little. I am Dr. Clementine Rook, and I note it here so that no household in Emberwick need be frightened as Miss Ivory's was.

Miss Ivory is the schoolmistress, the most sensible woman in the town. On Tuesday night she informed her sister that the roses on the wallpaper were nodding to her, and that she had nodded back to be polite. Later she set the ceiling a spelling lesson. Her sister sent for me at a run.

I found a hot forehead and a perfectly gentle patient. These fancies belong to the heat and go when it goes, leaving nothing behind. The remedy is a low lamp, a calm voice and a hand to hold. Arguing does no good. By morning Miss Ivory was cooler and remembered none of it. She was mortified about the ceiling, and asked me whether it had spelled well.

volumes.title: Pins in the Map
volumes.text:
Emberwick, the twentieth of November: fourteen cases of the lantern fever. Tonight I, Dr. Clementine Rook, pinned a map of the town to my study wall and pushed in a pin for every sickbed.

The town already has its explanation. It is the marsh mist, people say, creeping up the river at night. But my pins do not agree. The cottages at the marsh end, which get the mist first and thickest, have no fever at all. Nor do the pins follow the river.

They gather instead around Lamp Lane, in the middle of the town, like bees about a hive. In Lamp Lane stand the school, the bakery and eleven houses. A fever does not drift about like weather. It is handed from one person to the next, and somewhere in that lane it is being handed on. I do not yet see how. I have left the map where I can look at it.

volumes.title: The Turning
volumes.text:
Every fever has a turning, and with the lantern fever it comes on the third or fourth night. I am Dr. Clementine Rook of Emberwick. I watched it tonight in Mr. Hobb, the school caretaker, and I write it down while the candle lasts.

Near midnight he was at his hottest, dry and muttering. Then, within a quarter of an hour, his forehead grew damp. Soon he was wet through, as if he had been out in rain. The red went out of his cheeks. His breathing slowed and deepened, and he slept: real sleep, the first in three days.

That is the fire going out, its work finished. All that is wanted is a dry nightshirt, dry sheets and quiet. His wife and I changed the bed around him and he never stirred. Then he began to snore. I know of no pleasanter sound in my profession, and we sat and listened to it for some time.

volumes.title: Legs Like Wet String
volumes.text:
The lantern fever leaves in a night, but it does not give back the patient's strength at once. I am Dr. Clementine Rook of Emberwick, and the hardest part of my month has been keeping the recovered in their chairs.

After the fever turns, there is a week of weakness. The head is clear and the appetite is stirring, so the patient feels well, right up until standing. Then the legs go like wet string. It is only the body asking for time to restock the larder, and rest gives it.

Nobody believes me. Mrs. Dunnock went back to the bakery on her second day up and was found sitting down in the flour bin. Tam Weller got as far as the ferry landing and was carried home by his father. Miss Ivory tried to mark a pile of slates and woke with chalk on her cheek. All three are now resting under protest, and all three are mending.

volumes.title: The Tin Cup
volumes.text:
The twenty-fourth of November. Tonight I, Dr. Clementine Rook, believe I have found how the lantern fever goes about Emberwick. Twenty-six pins stand in my map, crowded around Lamp Lane, and I went through my casebook asking one question of each.

Every case is a child at the Lamp Lane school, or lives with one, or works there. Miss Ivory teaches there. Mr. Hobb sweeps there. Mrs. Dunnock, who puzzled me, carries bread to the school each morning, and she tells me she always stops at the pump in the yard for a drink.

At that pump hangs a single tin cup on a chain. Thirty-one children and anyone passing drink from it, lip after lip, all day. I cannot prove it, but I can act on it. I have asked Miss Ivory that every child bring a cup from home, and wash hands before dinner. The tin cup is now in my desk drawer.

volumes.title: The Doctor's Own Fever
volumes.text:
I write this in bed. On the first of December I, Dr. Clementine Rook, having attended thirty-three cases of the lantern fever in Emberwick, became the thirty-fourth. I am now able to describe it from the inside, which is thorough of me.

The shiver came first, and I was exactly as cold as my patients said and I had not quite believed. Then the heat. I asked for the window wider and then accused it of staring. My neighbour Mrs. Plover nursed me with sips of water, a cool cloth and no nonsense. On the third night, I am told, I lectured the bedpost on its pulse.

Then the turning: the sweat, the dry sheets, and a sleep like falling into a haystack. Today my head is clear and my legs are string. Mrs. Plover has hidden my boots. I mean to obey my own advice for a week, having learned how it feels to be given it.

volumes.title: The First Boiled Egg
volumes.text:
The last stage of the lantern fever is hunger, and it is the pleasantest to record. I am Dr. Clementine Rook of Emberwick, a fortnight on from my own sickbed, and I remember wanting a boiled egg more than I have ever wanted anything.

Appetite returns in steps. First broth, then toast, then the egg, and then, about the tenth day, the patient is discovered in the pantry. I tell families to let it come at its own pace.

There is better news than eggs. Since the tin cup at the school pump was taken down, new cases have dwindled: eight in the first week, five in the next, then two, and none at all since the eleventh of December. Mr. Sallow the potter has made thirty-one small cups, each with a child's name painted under the glaze. They hang on pegs in the schoolroom. Tam Weller, the first to fall ill, was the first to drink from his.

volumes.title: The Lantern Goes Out
volumes.text:
Midwinter Eve, and I, Dr. Clementine Rook, close this book. The lantern fever came to Emberwick on the eighth of November with Tam Weller's red cheeks, and the last patient, Mr. Sallow the potter, got out of bed this morning. Forty-one cases in six weeks. Forty-one recoveries. I have counted the columns twice for the pleasure of it.

I have set down all I saw: the shiver, the heat, the thirst, the dreams, the turning, the weakness and the hunger. A fever is a fire that knows its business. My part was water, cool cloths, clean sheets, and noticing a tin cup.

Tonight the town walked in the Midwinter procession, every child carrying a lantern, and Tam Weller at the front. I have taken the pins out of my map and rolled it away. The lamps going past my window were the only red faces in Emberwick, and they were made of paper.
